title: Melochia concatenata: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Melochia concatenata in Rice: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Melochia concatenata, or marasaluyot, is a perennial weed of rainfed palay. Learn to spot its star hairs and flower heads and keep it out of rice.
excerpt: Melochia concatenata is a branched, perennial broadleaf weed that farmers call Bankalanan, kaliñgan or marasaluyot. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it by its star shaped hairs and crowded flower heads, and how to control it before it sets seed.

heroImage.alt: Melochia concatenata, a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Jeevan Jose, Kerala, India, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This weed comes from the family Sterculiaceae, the same plant family as cacao. It has no common English name, so people use its scientific name, Melochia concatenata. In the bukid, farmers call it Bankalanan, kaliñgan or marasaluyot. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will see it in rainfed lowland rice fields. As a perennial, the same plant can live past one season if no one removes it. Seed is how it spreads. After flowering, it forms small, flattened round capsules that hold the seeds, and these fall to the ground when ripe. Plants left on bunds and field edges keep feeding seed into the paddy.

Look for branched stems that stand upright or spread out. Up close, the stems carry scattered hairs shaped like tiny stars. The leaves are oblong to oval, with a pointed tip and a broad, rounded or heart shaped base. As a broadleaf weed, it has wide leaves with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. Its flowers sit crowded in heads at the stem tips or leaf angles. Petals are white, sometimes pink or pale purple.

items: Branched stems that stand upright or spread out over the ground.
Scattered hairs shaped like tiny stars on the stems, best seen up close.
Oblong to oval leaves with a pointed tip and a rounded or heart shaped base.
Crowded flower heads at the stem tips or where leaves meet the stem.
White petals, sometimes pink or pale purple, mixed with thin, narrow bracts.
Flattened, round seed capsules forming after the flowers fade.

blocks.text:
Melochia concatenata competes with palay for water, fertilizer and light. Its branched stems spread out and shade nearby rice hills, most of all in the first weeks after planting. In rainfed fields, where moisture is often short, this fight for water hurts the rice even more.

Because it is a perennial, a plant that survives one season can come back bigger the next. Each plant also adds seed to the soil. Some seed can get mixed into the harvest and into palay saved for planting. Weeds like this also offer shelter to some insect pests between the rice hills.

items: Pull plants with their whole root, because this perennial can sprout again from a base left in the soil.
Check bunds and field edges after harvest, since perennial plants there survive the off season and seed into the next crop.
Weed before the crowded flower heads turn into round capsules, so the plant cannot add seed to the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Melochia concatenata down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Melochia concatenata Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Melochia concatenata

items.q: What is Melochia concatenata called in local dialects?
items.a: Farmers call it Bankalanan, kaliñgan or marasaluyot. It has no common English name, so many people use the scientific name. Local names can change from one province to the next. To be sure, look for star shaped hairs on the stems and crowded heads of white, pink or pale purple flowers.

items.q: How do I control this weed in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and good land preparation, and keep water in the field where you can. Pull young plants early with their whole root. Clean the bunds after harvest so no old plants remain. If you need a herbicide, pick one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice, and follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does it come back after I cut it?
items.a: It is a perennial. When you cut the stems but leave the root in the soil, the plant can sprout again. It also drops seed from its round capsules, so new plants keep coming up. That is why pulling the whole plant works better than cutting, and why the bunds need cleaning too.
